The basal metabolic rate of the Golden spiny mouse (Acomys russatus) has been quantified through controlled respirometry trials, revealing a maximum oxygen consumption of 40.84 milliliters per hour [JOi = 40.84 milliliters per hour] when measurements were conducted at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This metabolic value, reflecting the species' capacity for thermoregulation under resting conditions, is characteristic of a small desert-adapted rodent facing the energetic challenges of an arid environment. Newborn pups, which are altricial at the time of parturition, exhibit a modest wet weight at birth of 7 grams [Wwb = 7 grams] that underscores the rapid developmental trajectory required for survival in their xeric habitat. The contrast between the substantial maternal investment in gestation and the relatively small size of the neonate points to a life-history strategy balanced between litter size and offspring quality, a pattern observed in other members of the genus Acomys.

Reproductive output in Acomys russatus is characterized by a maximum rate of 2.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2.5 pups per litter] under optimal captive conditions maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Females typically produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a value derived from the sustained thermal conditions typical of their native rocky habitats. This species exhibits a comparatively rapid reproductive cycle for a murid rodent of its body size. The combination of moderate litter size and relatively short intervals between parturition events enables populations to recover quickly after periods of environmental stress, a crucial adaptation for life in the unpredictable precipitation regimes of the Eastern Desert and surrounding regions.

Gestation in the Golden spiny mouse lasts approximately 34 days [tg = approximately 34 days] when females are maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], a duration that aligns with values reported for other spiny mouse species. Following parturition, the weaning period is relatively brief, with offspring achieving nutritional independence from maternal milk at 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This rapid transition from suckling juvenile to independent feeding stages reflects the precocial nature of Acomys pups, which are born with open eyes and developed fur compared to many other murids. The early weaning age reduces the energetic burden on the lactating female, potentially allowing for a shorter inter-birth interval and thus higher overall lifetime fecundity in this seasonally breeding species.

When housed at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], captive-reared individuals reach sexual maturation at 91 days after birth [tp = 91 days after birth], a relatively early milestone compared to other desert rodents of similar body size. This trait, combined with the short gestation and weaning periods, contributes to a rapid generational turnover that is advantageous in fluctuating desert environments. Females ultimately attain an adult wet weight of 54.4 grams [Wwi = 54.4 grams], notably larger than male conspecifics in many populations, suggesting sexual size dimorphism linked to reproductive demands. The ultimate body size is reached after a period of consistent growth following the onset of reproductive maturity, with energetic resources increasingly directed toward meeting basal maintenance requirements and future reproductive effort as individuals age.

Longevity data for Acomys russatus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3.8 years [am = approximately 3.8 years] at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C] under captive conditions, a relatively extended duration for a small-bodied murid rodent. The species is known for its remarkable regenerative capabilities, including the ability to heal skin wounds without scarring, a trait that may confer survival advantages over its lifespan. Field studies suggest that mortality in natural populations is heavily influenced by predation pressure from diurnal raptors and snakes, while senescence in captive colonies typically manifests as gradual declines in fecundity and metabolic efficiency during the final year of life. This combination of traits positions the Golden spiny mouse as an intriguing subject for studies of both life-history evolution and tissue regeneration among desert-adapted mammals.
